data.title: Anthropic IPO faces test after recent selloff: What Wall Street experts are saying
data.description:
Anthropic's highly anticipated initial public offering is facing a difficult test as a sharp selloff in artificial intelligence stocks raises questions about its proposed $1.5 trillion valuation and the timing of the listing.

The AI company, which is preparing to go public as early as November, had been expected to pursue an offering of around $100 billion. 

However, prospective investors are increasingly questioning whether the proposed valuation reflects the company's financial prospects, particularly given its substantial commitments to computing infrastructure.

The market backdrop has also deteriorated.

An unwinding of AI-related investments has hit technology stocks, while political uncertainty following the US midterm elections has raised concerns about the future of data-centre construction.

The Wall Street Journal reported that at least three major investors believe Anthropic may have to lower its valuation, with one suggesting a figure closer to $1 trillion.

The growing resistance presents a challenge for one of the most closely watched IPOs in the technology sector.

Anthropic must balance investor expectations against its substantial funding requirements as it continues expanding its Claude AI models and securing computing capacity.

Anthropic IPO faces growing resistance to $1.5 trillion valuation

The proposed $1.5 trillion valuation has emerged as one of the biggest sticking points in Anthropic's IPO preparations.

Investors who had previously viewed the company as a must-own name are becoming more cautious as technology stocks come under pressure.

According to The Wall Street Journal, three major investors planning to participate in the offering believe Anthropic will probably need to reduce its valuation.

One investor reportedly suggested that the company could be worth closer to $1 trillion.

The company may also have to settle for a smaller fundraising target.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Anthropic could seek around $80 billion rather than the previously anticipated $100 billion.

The valuation debate comes as investors await further details about the company's financial performance.

Anthropic's amended S-1 filing showed that its revenue reached $17 billion in the third quarter.

Its revenue run rate, a measure used to estimate annual revenue based on current performance, exceeded $80 billion at the end of October, according to The Wall Street Journal.

However, investors are also looking beyond revenue growth to examine the costs associated with developing and operating increasingly sophisticated AI models.

Reuters reported that some prospective investors are waiting for Anthropic's October financial results before pushing for a lower valuation.

The company's October revenue figure was left blank in its updated S-1 filing, making it another important number for investors to assess.

The roadshow was initially expected to begin during the week of November 9, with pricing anticipated the following week, Reuters previously reported.

AI stock selloff and data-centre backlash complicate IPO plans

The deteriorating market environment has added another layer of uncertainty to Anthropic's listing.

A sharp selloff in technology stocks has raised questions about whether investors will be willing to support a $1.5 trillion valuation for an AI company at a time when enthusiasm around the sector is weakening.

The Global X Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF fell 6.2% during Thursday's session, reflecting the pressure on AI-related investments.

The political environment has also become more complicated.

Democratic victories in the US midterm elections have raised concerns about potential resistance to new data-centre developments.

Newly elected Democratic governors in states including Texas, Georgia and Ohio could create obstacles for construction projects.

Analysts at Jefferies cut their forecast for new data-centre capacity in 2030 by approximately 8% in a research note on Thursday.

This matters considerably for Anthropic because its business strategy depends on securing sufficient computing capacity to train and operate its Claude models.

In its IPO prospectus, the company acknowledged that political or financial developments that restrict data-centre capacity could pose a risk to its operations.

However, Malik Ahmed Khan, senior equity analyst at Morningstar, does not believe the current market weakness will derail the IPO.

"We don’t expect any near-term impact on the IPO," Khan wrote in a research note on Thursday.

He added that concerns surrounding data-centre development could become an interesting dynamic to watch over the next couple of years.

Khan also argued that developers could respond to local opposition by making greater investments in communities and introducing commitments to protect residents from rising electricity bills.

The continued presence of President Donald Trump in the White House could also make federal legislation restricting AI development more difficult, he added.

Michael Burry questions Anthropic's computing commitments

While the market selloff has raised concerns about Anthropic's valuation, the company's spending commitments have become another major source of investor scrutiny.

Michael Burry, the investor known for his bets against the US housing market before the 2008 financial crisis, has expressed reservations about participating in Anthropic's IPO.

In a Substack post on Wednesday, Burry highlighted the company's amended S-1 filing, particularly its commitments to spending on computing infrastructure.

The filing revealed that Anthropic has committed approximately $895.4 billion towards AI computing power, chips and other infrastructure required to develop and operate its models.

Burry argued that these commitments could become difficult to justify even if the company achieves the revenue growth anticipated by optimistic investors.

He pointed out that bullish investors expect Anthropic's revenue to reach around $100 billion in the coming year, a figure that remains substantially below its long-term infrastructure commitments.

In his assessment, the company's future spending commitments exceed bullish revenue expectations by roughly 12 times.

"Not only is the company priced for optimism," Burry wrote, "it is betting its entire existence on that optimism."

He also raised concerns about take-or-pay agreements with major hyperscalers.

Under these arrangements, Anthropic could be required to pay for computing capacity even when it does not need it.

This could increase operating costs and weaken its competitiveness against other AI model developers.

Burry said investors might not yet fully appreciate the implications of these commitments for Anthropic and the wider AI sector.

"The market is paying attention, but I fear the full realization of what has happened here will only be self-evident in the rear-view," he wrote.

"I have no plans to pursue shares of Anthropic, and I do not expect to be a shareholder anytime soon."

His position marks a shift from his earlier assessment of the company.

In April 2026, Burry had described Anthropic as "eating Palantir's lunch" and suggested that the market was moving towards a plug-and-play system for integrating AI models, which could benefit Claude.

Anthropic needs IPO proceeds to fund its AI ambitions

Despite the growing investor concerns, Anthropic has significant reasons to proceed with its planned listing.

The company has nearly $900 billion in short- and long-term supply commitments for chips and computing capacity.

Meeting these commitments will require substantial financial resources as it continues expanding its AI operations.

According to the company's prospectus, Anthropic had $146.6 billion in cash and other liquid assets.

However, postponing the IPO would temporarily prevent it from raising additional capital through the public markets.

The potential fundraising target of $80 billion to $100 billion would provide additional financial flexibility as the company competes in the increasingly capital-intensive AI industry.

However, investors are unlikely to support the offering simply because Anthropic needs the money.

Jim Lebenthal, chief market strategist at Cerity Partners, said in a Barron's report that the company could reconsider its plans if the market environment prevents it from achieving an attractive valuation.

He previously argued that Anthropic could instead raise capital in private markets if the public-market valuation fell too far.

HSBC's Max Kettner, who recently reduced his equity rating from maximum overweight to neutral, also identified Anthropic's IPO as a potentially significant event for financial markets.

"The real risk clearing event is probably the Anthropic IPO in two weeks, if it happens," Kettner said in an interview with Bloomberg News.

He suggested that a valuation closer to $1 trillion could be more acceptable to investors than the previously discussed $1.5 trillion figure.

Kettner also cautioned that the company would need to avoid a sharp decline immediately after listing.

"You come with a reasonably low valuation, such that in the secondary market you actually start rallying. Or at least not dumping 20-30% in the first week — because that obviously would be horrible."

The comments highlight the challenge facing Anthropic as it prepares for one of the largest potential public offerings in the technology industry.

A lower valuation could improve investor appetite and reduce the risk of a weak market debut.

However, it could also mean raising less capital than initially anticipated.

Ultimately, Anthropic's IPO will test whether public-market investors are still willing to pay a substantial premium for leading AI companies despite concerns about infrastructure costs, capital commitments and the sustainability of the sector's growth.

Read our in-depth guides on how to invest in Anthropic and how to buy Anthropic pre-IPO.

data.title: Anthropic IPO news: Valuation slips to $1.5 trillion as AI Bubble Index rises
data.description:
Anthropic's IPO faces major headwinds, with the company expected to go public at a significantly lower valuation than initially anticipated amid the ongoing jitters in the artificial intelligence (AI) industry. 

Anthropic IPO Could See a Valuation Cut to $1.5 Trillion

It has been a tumultuous period for companies in the artificial intelligence industry, with many of them seeing their valuations dive. Nvidia stock has moved into a correction after falling by double digits from its all-time high. The same is happening with other popular names like AMD, CoreWeave, and IREN. 

The ongoing retreat has had a major impact on Anthropic, the biggest AI lab in the world, as it considers going public. According to the WSJ, the company’s investors believe that it will be hard for the company to achieve the record $2 trillion valuation it was aiming for. 

These concerns jumped after the stock market crashed on Thursday, with the Nasdaq 100 sinking into a correction. The S&P 500 and Dow Jones also dropped substantially after the Democrats won the midterm election convincingly. 

The WSJ report notes that the eventual valuation will be about $1.5 trillion, with some investors expecting it to be about $1 trillion. 

This valuation makes Anthropic the fastest-growing company to cross the $1 trillion mark. In contrast, it took decades for companies like Amazon, Nvidia, Berkshire Hathaway, and Alphabet to cross that valuation.

Anthropic S1 Document Showcased Growing Revenues But Substantial Risks

The recently released S1 document showed that Anthropic’s business is doing well, with the revenue growth accelerating. It made $17 billion in the third quarter, with the number of customers growing substantially. 

However, the report also showed that the company faces some substantial risks ahead. One of the key risks is that Anthropic’s losses jumped in the quarter, reaching a high of $23 billion. $21.9 billion of this was due to a non-cash charge related to the value of its convertible bonds.

Another risk is that most of the company’s revenue comes from a handful of clients. This means that its growth would be affected if one or more of these companies decided to move to other AI companies.

Anthropic is also spending billions of dollars in computing deals by companies like CoreWeave, Nscale, and SpaceX. This means that it will take some time for it to become free cash flow positive. 

Further, there are concerns that the AI business will flop, with the AI Stock Bubble Index rising to 74. Some popular analysts, including Ray Dalio and Ken Griffin have warned that the bubble may burst soon as interest rates rise. Yesterday’s strong nonfarm payrolls(NFP) data suggests that the Fed will deliver another rate hike in December.

SpaceX IPO Trends Points to Risk to ANT Stock

Meanwhile, investors are concerned about Anthropic following the hyped SpaceX IPO. While the stock initially jumped, it then plunged to $105, costing investors over $1 trillion. Its attempts to rebound faced substantial resistance at $176. As such, investors are concerned that the ANT stock will also drop.

Indeed, data shows that most of the recent IPOs have flopped. For example, Circle Internet Group initially surged to $300 after its IPO last year. Since then, it has dropped to $67 as its revenue growth has stalled. 

Similarly, CoreWeave initially surged to $186.7 after its IPO last year and then retreated to the current $46. Gemini Space Station rose to $46 and then dropped to $2.46 today.

data.title: DraftKings stock just lost 20%: the real story isn't the earnings miss
data.description:
DraftKings (DKNG) shares opened sharply lower on Friday after the sports betting giant reported its fiscal Q3 earnings that missed Wall Street estimates and lowered its full-year guidance as well.

Revenue came in at $1.329 billion versus expectations of about $1.39 billion, while adjusted losses were also deeper than analysts had forecast.

Investors reacted swiftly, wiping billions from DKNG’s market cap. But the headline numbers tell only part of the story.

The bigger question for shareholders is whether DraftKings is “deliberately” sacrificing near-term profitability to pursue a potentially much larger opportunity in prediction markets.

DraftKings earnings miss is a strategy reset

At first glance, DraftKings release gave investors plenty of reasons to hit the sell button. The firm’s adjusted EBITDA slipped into negative territory as spending accelerated.

Plus, management reduced its sales ($6.35 billion to $6.55 billion) and EBITDA outlook as well.

Yet, what stands out is not weak customer demand. Monthly unique payers came in up 13% to 41 million, and average revenue per user increased to $109.

Those are not metrics typically associated with a fading business.

Instead, DKNG is making a conscious decision to redirect significant resources toward Predictions – its rapidly expanding prediction-markets platform.

In other words, investors were not simply reacting to missed estimates.

They were reacting to the realization that DraftKings is entering a new investment cycle, one that could weigh on profits far longer than Wall Street previously anticipated.

Significance of Predictions for DKNG shares

The most revealing part of the earnings release was buried behind the disappointing guidance.

Management disclosed that more than 1.6 million customers have engaged with its new Predictions offering this year – while annualized prediction-market consumer volume reached $10.1 billion in October.

The company said it has already become the third-largest predictions exchange by total volume.

Those figures help explain why executives are willing to accept hundreds of millions of dollars in additional investment.

Prediction markets sit at the intersection of sports betting, financial markets, and event forecasting, opening an entirely new revenue stream beyond traditional wagering.

For investors, this changes the valuation debate. DraftKings can no longer be viewed solely as a sports betting operator.

Increasingly, the stock is becoming a bet on management's ability to build a dominant platform in an emerging market that remains largely untapped.

The challenge is that such opportunities are difficult to model, making near-term earnings visibility much lower.

What DraftKings stock investors should watch next?

The irony of this sell-off is that the earnings report may have strengthened the long-term bull case even as it damaged short-term sentiment.

DraftKings introduced 2027 revenue guidance of $7.35 billion to $7.75 billion and forecast adjusted EBITDA of $800 million to $1.0 billion despite continuing investment in Predictions.

That suggests management sees today's spending less as an expense and more as customer acquisition for a business it believes can become materially larger over time.

The market, however, is demanding proof before granting that benefit of the doubt.

Going forward, three metrics matter more than quarterly earnings beats or misses: growth in prediction-market users, the pace of trading volume expansion, and evidence that those customers can be monetized profitably.

If those indicators continue trending upward, this week's plunge could eventually look like a temporary reaction to transition costs.

If they stall, investors may conclude that DraftKings traded a highly profitable future for an expensive experiment. For now, Wall Street is voting with caution.

data.title: Micron stock rebounds 5% after huge selloff even as AI demand risks persist
data.description:
Micron Technology shares MU are recovering after Thursday’s sharp technology selloff, but questions remain over whether the memory-chip maker’s low valuation reflects an investment opportunity or the risk of a downturn in AI-related demand.

The stock gained 5.8% on Friday after plunging 17% in the previous session.

At Thursday’s closing price, Micron traded at just 3.7 times its estimated fiscal 2027 earnings, according to FactSet.

That valuation appears particularly low given expectations that the company will more than double its revenue and earnings in the current fiscal year, with further growth forecast for the following year.

However, memory-chip companies often trade at low earnings multiples near the peak of their cycles, when profits are elevated.

Micron's low valuation faces memory-cycle risks

The main concern is whether demand for memory chips used in artificial intelligence servers could weaken sooner than expected.

The potential slowdown in data-centre construction following Democratic victories in the US midterm elections has raised questions about the sustainability of AI infrastructure spending.

A downturn in memory demand, previously expected in 2028 or later, could arrive earlier if data-centre investment slows.

Micron has some protection against this risk through long-term take-or-pay agreements covering more than 35% of its forecast revenue through 2030.

The contracts require customers to pay for agreed supplies, potentially reducing the impact of normal fluctuations in memory-chip supply and demand.

However, there are concerns that customers could seek to renegotiate these agreements during a downturn in AI spending.

Similar contracts across the semiconductor industry during the supply shortages caused by the Covid pandemic were later renegotiated to maintain customer relationships.

Micron has received close to $32 billion in cash deposits under its agreements, but the durability of the contracts remains an important consideration for investors.

Buybacks could support Micron shares

The company also has the option of using share repurchases to support its stock. Micron can begin major buybacks from December 9.

Barron's estimates the company could repurchase $100 billion of its shares during its current fiscal year, which ends in August 2027. That amount would represent more than 10% of its current market value.

The potential scale of the buyback programme could provide another factor for investors assessing the stock's valuation, although its execution will depend on the company's capital allocation decisions.

Analysts divided on AI infrastructure outlook

Analyst views on semiconductor valuations and AI spending remain mixed.

UBS analyst Nicolas Gaudois argues that valuations for Micron's South Korean peers, SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, indicate that markets are already pricing in a downturn in memory prices in 2028.

He estimates a risk-reward profile for the two companies that implies 160% potential upside over the next 12 months against 30% downside.

Micron trades at only a slightly higher valuation than the South Korean companies, suggesting a broadly similar scenario.

Raymond James Chief Investment Officer Larry Adam also remains positive on AI infrastructure.

He believes some semiconductor and AI stocks are trading at discounts of around 30% to historical valuations and expects earnings growth to remain healthy.

He therefore favours gradually rebuilding exposure to technology and semiconductor stocks.

However, Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives has become more cautious.

He now expects 10% fewer data centres in his baseline forecast, with potential reductions reaching 15% to 20%.

He also expects Big Tech capital spending growth to peak in 2027, earlier than previously anticipated.

Ives believes AI infrastructure projects are more likely to face delays than outright cancellations.

His preference has consequently shifted towards software stocks over semiconductor companies.

data.title: Fed rate hike odds jump after October jobs report as officials signal more tightening
data.description:
Traders are increasing their bets on another Federal Reserve interest rate hike in December after a stronger-than-expected October employment report showed that the US labor market remains resilient.

The chance of a December rate hike rose to 77%, up about 10 percentage points from Thursday, according to CME FedWatch data.

The repricing suggests investors are becoming increasingly concerned that the central bank may need to tighten monetary policy further rather than pause its rate increases.

Job report comes in hot

The Labor Department reported on Friday that US employers added 165,000 jobs in October, more than double economists' expectations of 65,000.

The unemployment rate also declined to 4.1% from 4.2%, while average hourly earnings increased 0.4% month over month, marking their strongest monthly gain since January.

Labor Department revisions also added a total of 84,000 new jobs to the August and September totals.

The stronger labour market data pushed Treasury yields higher with the benchmark 10-year note rising four basis points to 4.88.

The latest numbers followed the Federal Reserve's decision last week to leave its benchmark interest rate unchanged in a range of 3.75% to 4%, after raising it in September.

The October employment data have strengthened expectations that policymakers could resume tightening as they continue to battle inflation.

Fed officials signal more rate increases

Comments from several Federal Reserve officials this week have reinforced expectations that borrowing costs may need to move higher.

Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack said on Thursday that monetary policy would need to become restrictive to bring inflation back to the central bank's 2% target.

"I expect that monetary policy will need to move to a restrictive stance to bring inflation back to 2% in a timely manner," Hammack said.

She favored smaller and more frequent rate adjustments, arguing that a gradual approach would be less disruptive to households, businesses and financial markets.

She also warned that delayed action could allow inflation expectations to become entrenched.

Hammack, along with Fed Governor Lisa Cook, voted in favor of a rate hike last week.

Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin echoed those concerns, saying inflation remained too high and was holding steady rather than declining.

"Inflation is too high. That means the path is pretty straightforward. The question, of course, is pace,” Barkin told CNBC.

New York Fed President John Williams struck a somewhat similar tone on Friday.

While acknowledging that inflation remains elevated, he suggested policymakers should assess incoming data before deciding on further action.

"Inflation is absolutely too high. It's been too high for too long," Williams said at a European Central Bank conference in Frankfurt.

The latest jobs figures have strengthened the case for higher borrowing costs, but the wage data offer a more complicated picture.

Although monthly earnings accelerated, annual wage growth stood at 3.1%, remaining below inflation for the seventh consecutive month.

Investors will continue monitoring inflation, employment and energy prices for clues about the Fed's next move.

data.title: Do billion-dollar crypto hacks threaten the industry's mainstream ambitions?
data.description:
Cryptocurrency has spent the past few years making considerable progress towards institutional acceptance.

Bitcoin exchange-traded funds have opened the market to traditional investors, banks are exploring digital-asset services, and governments have begun establishing regulatory frameworks for parts of the industry.

But a series of increasingly expensive security breaches at major exchanges is raising questions about whether that progress is translating into broader confidence.

The latest incident involved Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, which suffered a security breach on October 29 that resulted in approximately $6.3 billion worth of digital assets being stolen.

Attackers compromised infrastructure used to authorise withdrawals, with Binance's initial investigation pointing to a potentially compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer.

The exchange said it found no evidence that wallet private keys had been leaked.

The incident followed a $388 million breach at Bitget in September 2026 and the $1.5 billion theft from Bybit in February 2025.

The Bybit incident was the largest cryptocurrency theft on record at the time.

The Binance breach subsequently surpassed it, highlighting the scale of the security failures confronting even the industry's largest platforms.

The market reaction was immediate. Bitcoin fell below $78,000, hitting its lowest level in six weeks after the Binance incident, while Ether reached a two-month low.

Customers also withdrew billions of dollars from Binance after withdrawals resumed.

Yet the price reaction and the scale of the theft do not necessarily establish how much confidence has been lost, or whether prospective investors are becoming less willing to enter the market.

The more consequential question is whether crypto's growing institutional legitimacy is developing alongside, or ahead of, the public confidence needed to sustain mainstream adoption.

Are repeated security breaches creating a trust problem?

Michael Tanguma, Co-founder and CEO of Bitcoin custody provider Onramp, said that the distinction between the underlying asset and the institutions holding it is central to understanding the problem.

"They (the hacks) are undermining confidence in intermediaries, which is not the same as undermining confidence in the asset," Tanguma said.

He argued that people who haven't entered the cryptocurrency market may care less about whether Bitcoin's underlying network functions as intended than about finding a reliable place to hold their assets.

"What they doubt is whether there is a safe place to hold it, and every breach confirms that doubt," he told Invezz.

The distinction is important for an industry that frequently separates vulnerabilities in exchanges and custodians from the technology underpinning individual cryptocurrencies.

A compromised exchange wallet does not necessarily indicate a failure of the Bitcoin network.

But that technical distinction may be less obvious to someone whose first exposure to digital assets is a headline about billions of dollars being stolen.

Bill Zielke, Chief Revenue Officer at BitPay, made a similar point.

"If you lose money, you don't care which layer failed," he said, arguing that customers need to trust the companies holding their assets as much as the technology itself.

"Repeated security breaches can undermine investor confidence, particularly with people who were already skeptical," he added.

Professor Iwa Salami, Professor of Financial Law and Regulation and Director of the Centre of FinTech at the University of East London, believes the consequences are unevenly distributed.

"Retail confidence suffers most. Institutions are more resilient because they can choose what to touch," she said.

Institutional investors can set limits on their exposure, conduct due diligence and select regulated custodians.

Individual investors generally have fewer resources and less negotiating power when assessing the security arrangements of an exchange or service provider.

"Repeated hacks, exploits and collapses reinforce the view that crypto is a space where consumers bear losses with no recourse," the professor told Invezz.

Salami said recurring failures involving governance, key management and operational controls pointed towards shortcomings in the industry's regulatory framework rather than isolated incidents.

The concern is not necessarily that every exchange breach will cause investors to abandon cryptocurrencies.

It is that repeated incidents could reinforce existing doubts among people who have yet to become participants.

Are investors actually losing confidence?

Establishing whether security breaches are causing a lasting deterioration in confidence is more difficult than tracking Bitcoin's price or measuring withdrawals from an exchange.

Binance's experience offers an early indication of the distinction.

Customers withdrew a net $4.72 billion from the exchange after withdrawals resumed following the October breach.

That represented approximately 3% of the platform's assets, while Binance co-chief executive Richard Teng said on November 3 that customer inflows and outflows had largely normalised.

The exchange also said it had replenished 98% of the affected tokens, using its Secure Asset Fund for Users and other company resources to cover the losses.

The outflows demonstrate that customers responded to the incident, but they do not establish a widespread departure from the platform or a lasting decline in confidence across the broader market.

Nor do exchange withdrawals capture people who decide against buying cryptocurrency in the first place.

Research commissioned by the National Cryptocurrency Association and conducted by Harris Poll offers some insight into that group.

Its 2026 Crypto Readiness Report surveyed 2,014 Americans who did not own cryptocurrency.

It found that 43% cited concerns about security and fraud as a barrier to ownership, while 31% identified a lack of trust in crypto platforms.

A lack of understanding was the most commonly cited obstacle, at 48%.

The survey was conducted between June 24 and July 1, before the Bitget and Binance incidents.

It therefore provides a baseline for existing concerns rather than evidence that those particular breaches have reduced adoption.

Academic research also points to a relationship between trust and cryptocurrency participation.

A study published in the Journal of Technology Transfer in November 2025 examined 1,519 individual investors across Denmark, Finland and Sweden.

It found that people who trusted strangers in financial matters were more likely to hold cryptocurrencies and express an intention to do so in the future.

Ylva Baeckström, a Senior Lecturer in Finance at King's College London and one of the study's co-authors, said limited knowledge about digital assets could make it harder for investors to distinguish between an asset and the service provider through which they access it.

"This muddles the difference between the asset value and the reliability of the service provider," she said.

The research, however, was based on survey data collected in November and December 2022, shortly after the collapse of FTX.

It does not measure the effect of the recent exchange breaches on investor behaviour.

HashKey Group's Tim Sun believes sustained participation provides a better measure of confidence than immediate price movements or withdrawals.

"Market prices can rebound well before trust is repaired," he said.

He suggested that user retention, new-user onboarding, net capital inflows, and longer-term participation in digital-asset applications would provide a clearer picture of whether confidence is recovering.

Wall Street is moving in. Is retail confidence keeping pace?

The apparent contrast between institutional participation and retail concerns is particularly relevant as the cryptocurrency industry becomes increasingly integrated into traditional financial markets.

The introduction of spot Bitcoin exchange-traded products in the US in January 2024 gave investors access to Bitcoin through conventional brokerage accounts.

Ether products followed, while subsequent changes to exchange-traded product listing standards widened the route for qualifying products backed by other digital assets.

The regulatory environment has also evolved.

President Donald Trump signed the GENIUS Act into law in July 2025, establishing a federal framework for payment stablecoins.

In October 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency issued a final rule implementing the legislation, covering requirements including reserves, redemption, risk management, and supervision.

The rule is scheduled to take effect on January 18, 2027. However, the broader regulatory picture remains incomplete.

The CLARITY Act, which seeks to establish a wider market-structure framework for digital assets, failed to advance in the Senate earlier this year.

For Salami, the speed of product development has outpaced some of the safeguards supporting it.

"Product access (ETFs, custody offerings, tokenisation pilots) has moved faster than the supporting infrastructure of standards, supervision and legal clarity," she said.

That gap does not necessarily prevent institutional capital from entering the market.

Institutions can gain exposure through products and service providers that operate within familiar financial and regulatory structures.

Sun argued that institutional investors do not need complete confidence in the wider cryptocurrency ecosystem to participate.

"Institutional adoption of digital assets does not necessarily rely on complete trust in the broader crypto ecosystem," he told Invezz.

Through regulated custodians, asset segregation and limits on counterparty exposure, institutions can isolate some of the risks associated with holding and trading digital assets.

But that transition can also create new vulnerabilities. As traditional financial institutions become gateways to digital assets, custody and operational risks could become concentrated among a smaller number of large providers.

Tanguma raised a similar concern, arguing that institutions will need clarity over what they legally own and how their assets are protected if a platform or custodian fails.

The distinction also extends to how people use cryptocurrencies.

Zielke said businesses could accept digital-asset payments through processors that convert receipts into local currency immediately, allowing merchants to serve crypto users without holding the underlying assets themselves.

"Taking a crypto payment is very different from keeping your net worth on an exchange," he told Invezz.

That suggests adoption can advance through payments and regulated investment products even when concerns about exchange custody remain unresolved.

What would it take to build confidence?

The debate ultimately extends beyond preventing individual security incidents.

It concerns what happens to customers when a platform fails and whether they have enforceable rights to recover their assets.

Salami argued that regulatory requirements should be based on the functions performed by digital-asset businesses, with clearer rules for custody, lending and trading.

She also called for stronger asset segregation, independent audits, cybersecurity testing and incident disclosures.

She questioned the reliance on exchange-operated protection funds, arguing that such arrangements are voluntary and depend on the financial strength of the companies maintaining them.

Most direct cryptocurrency holdings also do not receive the same statutory deposit protection available to eligible bank deposits or the brokerage protections provided by SIPC for qualifying securities and cash.

That leaves customers with a different set of protections from those available through traditional financial institutions.

Tanguma argued that custody arrangements should avoid single points of failure, including systems that allow one compromised employee or device to authorise transactions.

He advocated structures in which multiple independent parties must approve asset movements.

However, technical safeguards alone cannot resolve questions about legal ownership, compensation and responsibility.

Sun argued that the industry's objective should be to protect customers even when individual institutions fail, rather than asking investors to place their faith in a particular company.

"The ultimate objective should not be convincing investors that a specific institution is flawless, but rather building a resilient financial system where investor assets and rights remain well-protected even when individual institutions fail," he said.

Crypto's institutional expansion and its recurring security failures are not necessarily mutually exclusive.

The industry can attract capital through regulated products while individual investors remain cautious about the platforms and services through which they access digital assets.

Whether that divergence becomes a lasting obstacle to mainstream adoption will depend partly on whether the industry can demonstrate that customer assets, ownership rights, and avenues for recourse are protected when something goes wrong.

Institutional acceptance can open the door to a larger market. It does not, by itself, answer whether ordinary investors will feel comfortable walking through it.

data.title: iMerit’s Radha Basu on how AI is reshaping India’s data annotation jobs
data.description:
Data annotation jobs are becoming increasingly vital in providing jobs to people from tier 2 and 3 cities in India.

Data annotation jobs are where workers repeatedly feed data into AI models and direct them to understand it correctly.

India's data annotation tools market was worth $138 million in 2026 and is expected to reach $648 million in 2031, according to Ken Research.

While data annotation is currently providing job opportunities to a lot of people, there are fears that as models become more sophisticated, it will remove the need for the current workers in the field.

In a conversation with Invezz, Radha Ramaswami Basu, Executive Vice President and Head of iMerit, an EXL Company, discusses how the growing adoption of artificial intelligence is changing the nature of data annotation jobs rather than simply eliminating them.

She explains how workers in India's tier 2 and tier 3 cities can move from routine labelling tasks to specialised roles in model evaluation, red teaming and human oversight, while examining the opportunities and challenges facing India's AI workforce.

Invezz: There are many fears that AI is going to replace jobs, and that includes people who annotate data as models become more sophisticated and perfect. There are also fears that AI increases productivity, and fewer people are required to do a task that needed more people in the past. How would you respond to these claims? Could you provide a counterargument to this claim?

Realistically, no one has been able to state for sure how this will play out.

We can provide some observations from being a part of the industry with a focus on human experts and their role in the AI stack.

First, AI is heavily dependent on human input, human expertise, and human oversight.

We do not expect this to go away. But we expect that this will become more advanced, more nuanced and require both judgment and nuance.

In our own space, routine data labeling, such as drawing boxes around cars, is being automated.

People who previously did that work will need to move to harder tasks where the situations are more complex and multidimensional.

Instead of assessing whether something is a car in an image, the expert has to assess what actions the car may and should take or what to do if there is a sudden emergency.

The work becomes more descriptive and subjective, and checking the work becomes even more advanced. Knowing what “right answer” looks like becomes non-trivial.

As a model becomes more capable, the cost of its mistakes rises, and so does the need to check it.

A model that drafts emails needs light review. A model that approves a loan, reads a scan, or steers a car needs people who can show it was right.

Every model update also has to be evaluated again, because a fix in one area can break another.

Demand is moving toward expertise. A few years ago, most requests we received were for large teams to label images.

Today, clients increasingly ask for physicians to check a model’s clinical reasoning, lawyers to test its reading of a contract, and mathematicians to find the flaw in a proof.

Coders are writing fewer basic functions and instead are reviewing, correcting and approving more complex behaviours generated by AI.

A labor market is forming around expert judgment both in high tech and in the enterprise.

It demands speed, accuracy, and cognitive load, all having value in the market.

People with early experience who grow with it become super-valuable.

On productivity, history suggests that when a task gets cheaper, it gets used more.

Companies apply AI to more problems, more languages, and more countries, and each launch brings new evaluation needs.

The roles are changing faster than they are disappearing. Our job is to make sure people change with them.

Invezz: AI is expected to bring a lot of benefits to robotics. In your view, how quickly can robotics become sophisticated enough to start doing work that is currently dangerous for humans to do

Robots already do some of this work in repetitive, controlled settings, such as pipeline inspection, assembly plants, warehouse logistics, and handling chemical materials.

Now the next frontier is operating in unpredictable environments. A factory floor follows rules. A farm field, a mine, or a construction site changes every hour.

We worked with an agricultural robotics company to take its weeding system from early experiments to an advanced AI product.

Close to a million images were annotated over the engagement, and the system grew to recognize hundreds of plant types, with clear gains in detection accuracy and in how well it handled new conditions.

Better tooling and automation cut completion time for the most complex scenes by 61 percent, and real-time monitoring let the team spot and correct edge cases quickly. 

That last point is the strategic one.

The first 99 percent of training teaches a system what it will usually see.

The last 1 percent is where trust is earned: the weed that looks like a crop seedling, the plant half covered in mud, the field under harsh light.

A robot also has to combine camera, LiDAR, and other sensor data into one consistent picture of the same moment.

Data can look correct on a screen and still fail in the field. Human judgment tells the two apart.

Progress will come workflow by workflow. Narrow, repetitive work in tough conditions will move first, likely within the next few years.

Work that requires a robot to improvise will take longer. Until then, the most reliable setup is a robot doing the physical work with a human ready to step in remotely.

Invezz: India supplies a large share of the world's annotation workforce. As routine labeling gets automated, what happens to entry-level annotators in smaller cities? What does the career path look like from a basic labeling role to an expert evaluator, and how is iMerit helping people make that move?

Smaller cities are where much of India’s new work is happening.

The Quess Pulse Report for the first half of fiscal 2026 found that 69 percent of payroll-linked employment is in Tier 2 and Tier 3 cities.

Tier 3 towns alone account for 40 percent of the workforce and Tier 2 hubs for 29 percent, compared with 31 percent in Tier 1 cities. The future of AI work in India will be decided there.

Routine labeling is being automated, and entry-level roles are changing with it. Inside iMerit, four kinds of roles are growing:

  • Ground truth builders turn images, video, documents, sensor data, and medical scans into data a model can learn from. They also write the prompt and response pairs used to tune a model.
  • Model evaluators assess what a model produces, correct it, and track patterns of failure with every update.
  • Red teamers test a model in creative ways and document exactly where it fails, often across languages and cultures as AI reaches new countries.
  • Human in the loop experts step in once a model is live. When an AI system in insurance, finance, or medicine is uncertain, the decision comes to them.

A new team member now starts by checking and correcting what a model produces.

From there, people specialize in a field such as LiDAR, medical imaging, or a regional language, then move into evaluation, red teaming, and project leadership.

About 3,200 people work with us full-time, and 90 percent of them are in India.

Around that core is a network of more than 30,000 curated experts, our Scholars, who join projects when their expertise is needed.

The full-time team gives us consistency and quality over the long term. The Scholar network gives us reach into almost any field a model needs to learn.

The most important change in India is the kind of work being done.

For a global pharmaceutical company, pathologists in India handled first-pass annotation of tissue slides, and US subspecialists reviewed their work.

Indian talent is moving from processing data to shaping clinical judgment for global medicine. Across every role, expert judgment is what keeps AI safe and reliable.

Invezz: Your Scholars network includes physicians, linguists, scientists, and engineers. As models get better, does the value of human data go up or down, and why?

It goes up. Better models make more convincing mistakes.

A fluent answer to a medical or financial question can still be wrong, and catching it takes a physician or a mathematician with years of practice.

AI development is also shifting.

The focus is moving from building ever more capable foundation models to adapting them for specific uses, especially in regulated industries like healthcare, banking, and insurance.

That work depends on experts who can challenge a model before it reaches customers.

We call it tormenting models. We question the model, question it again to make sure it is working, and actually try to break it.

That is why we built the iMerit Scholars platform on Ango Hub.

Our community includes more than 30,000 vetted experts across 118 countries and 106 languages, and the platform is designed to grow to hundreds of thousands.

Every Scholar goes through a three-tier assessment. The first screens general AI capability and cognitive skills.

The second tests domain qualifications and the ability to work effectively with AI models. The most specialized roles add peer review by other experts in the field.

Being part of EXL gives us access to deeper healthcare and insurance expertise, which strengthens our ability to support AI built for specific enterprises.

Our biggest need right now is to go into new expertise, scale into newer languages, and into newer levels of the same expertise.

The next phase of generative AI will be won by those who treat expertise as human capital. Technology should make that expertise easier to reach, retain, and apply.

Invezz: In areas like healthcare AI and autonomous vehicles, a flawed training set can cause real harm. What does iMerit do to catch bias, errors, and blind spots in data before they reach a model?

Most harmful errors in training data are systematic.

A category is defined poorly, a condition is missing, or reviewers read the same thing in different ways. We focus on catching these patterns early, and the work starts with who checks the data and how.

In healthcare, the standard is clinical truth. Our open-source 3D mammography dataset, released in 2026, covers 558 patients, 271 with malignant findings and 287 with benign ones.

Every case is confirmed by biopsy and reviewed by US board-certified radiologists.

The average tumor is 1.34 cm, and 85 percent of lesions are under 2 cm.

This helps a model learn from early cancers, which are the hardest to detect. On every scan, a radiologist has marked the exact boundary between a lesion and healthy tissue.

That judgment is now part of the data. Fast Company recognized the dataset in its Next Big Things in Tech 2026 list. 

In autonomous mobility, the standard is consistency across people, sensors and regions.

On one program covering images, video and 3D LiDAR across the US, Europe and Asia Pacific, LiDAR accuracy was stuck near 80 percent.

Our specialists held weekly calibration sessions so reviewers made the same calls, and added a two-stage quality check.

They also revised the taxonomy, adding classes for road objects the model kept missing and removing ones that added noise. Accuracy rose above the client’s 95 percent threshold.

That’s the main reason clients choose to work with iMerit. In high-stakes situations, you want professionalism, accountability, and consistency.

Invezz: Will AI mostly benefit large labs and wealthy countries, or can it spread opportunity more widely? How can countries like India participate in AI as creators and shapers of models, and not just as a source of low-cost labor?

The foundations of AI, such as compute and capital, are concentrated today. The value of AI, however, depends on how well it understands the people it serves.

That understanding comes from everywhere.

A model becomes truly useful when it understands a patient’s history, a farmer’s soil, or a customer’s language.

That knowledge lives with doctors, agronomists, linguists and engineers around the world. 

India also has a long tradition of knowing how to do global business - listening to the customer; understanding the problem; solving the problem.

This is very important in applying high-stakes AI in the enterprise.

India brings a deep pool of scientific and professional talent, 22 scheduled languages and a large population whose needs AI must learn to serve.

The greatest opportunity lies in defining how models are evaluated, building datasets that reflect Indian realities, and developing domain models for healthcare, agriculture, and finance.

Those who set the standards will shape what AI becomes.

I have always believed that true breakthroughs happen at the intersection of people and machines. Countries that invest in both will help shape the future of AI.

Invezz: In 2026, iMerit was acquired by EXL. How does pairing your expert data network and Ango Hub platform with EXL's broader data and AI services change what you can offer clients? Where do you see the company’s future moving forward?

I see three directions ahead.

First, it brings frontier lab discipline to regulated industries.

EXL’s clients in insurance, banking, and healthcare will need to show regulators how their models were tested, who reviewed them, and how failures were handled.

iMerit has built that rigor through evaluation, red teaming, and RLHF with foundation model companies. Together, we can help enterprises become audit-ready before the rules arrive.

Second, it connects expert judgment to real workflows.

Ango Hub brings data, experts, and quality checks into one place.

EXL knows how claims, underwriting, and operations run every day. Together, we can tune models to a client’s own processes and data, and keep evaluating them once they are live.

That shortens the path from pilot to production.

Third, it widens where we can grow. iMerit’s work in robotics, autonomous mobility, healthcare AI, and physical AI gives EXL a direct role with foundation model and autonomy companies.

EXL’s scale of nearly 68,000 people gives us the depth to take on larger, longer programs.

Both companies were built the same way, with people at the center and domain expertise as the foundation of good AI.

That common ground is why the integration has felt natural from the start.


The post iMerit’s Radha Basu on how AI is reshaping India’s data annotation jobs appeared first on Invezz

data.title: Large-scale employee buyouts are not new, but big tech is changing its meaning
data.description:
In the early 2000s, mobile phones arrived. Soon, communicating through those clunky, stationary telephones was going out of fashion.

The future was here, and Verizon was not ready.

Customers were abandoning landlines for mobile phones in growing numbers.

The company’s traditional business, once a reliable engine of revenue, was steadily eroding.

Hit by regulatory setbacks amid already difficult conditions, Verizon turned to a familiar corporate instrument: the voluntary buyout.

It offered packages to roughly 152,000 employees.

A few years later, Ford did something similar, extending buyout offers to about 75,000 workers while deep in losses and fighting for survival.

These were two companies in structural trouble, trying to shrink their way toward stability.

For decades, large-scale voluntary separation programs carried a clear meaning. Companies were in distress and needed to cut costs.

That meaning is now changing.

Microsoft's hard decision

In late October 2026, Microsoft sent a different kind of message to a large share of its workforce.

Roughly 60,000 employees, about 27% of the company, received a voluntary exit offer.

It was the largest such program in Microsoft's history.

Sixty thousand is a staggering number. But an even more astonishing figure is $36.6 billion.

That was the company's net income in the three months ended September.

Microsoft reported its results just days after making the buyout offers public. The business was roaring.

Revenue reached $92.3 billion, up 19%. Operating income rose to $45.9 billion.

Net income climbed 32% to $36.6 billion. Azure grew 48%. Wall Street estimates were left behind.

On the same day, Alphabet posted its own strong quarter: revenue of $127.6 billion, up 25%, with Google Cloud more than doubling to $30.7 billion.

The company said it was now running at a half-trillion-dollar annual pace.

And yet, this week, Alphabet also confirmed that it was extending its existing buyout program to five more countries.

The financial profiles of both companies remain robust. And yet, they are increasingly turning to the same tool once reserved for periods of decline.

Meta has also used comparable packages in certain markets.

The approach of large-scale buyouts might not be new, but things are definitely changing.

A different way out

People who study how companies manage their workforces say the shift is revealing.

Wayne Cascio, who has researched downsizing for decades, says such exercises have been around since the 1970s. However, he, too, is seeing a shift.

"Voluntary buyouts started in the 1970s, primarily in manufacturing. During the global financial crisis in 2008, they were widely used by all kinds of companies," Cascio said in a recent Harvard Business Review interview.

"What's changing now is the types of people who are being offered buyouts. In the past, companies usually required employees to have reached a minimum age and minimum tenure — say, people over 55 with at least 10 years at the company.

"Effectively, that means most people were usually within a couple of years of qualifying for retirement. We called them buyouts, but they functioned as early retirement programs. Often, they included early vesting or other retirement sweeteners.

"Microsoft's buyouts have no age limitation and almost no tenure requirement. They're being offered to everyone in certain departments. That approach is becoming more common. Having so many people of all ages affected that's different from what we've seen before."

Why are companies choosing buyouts over outright layoffs?

Cascio explains that voluntary buyouts can give employees a greater sense of agency than abrupt job cuts. That sense of control can also help protect the morale of those who remain.

Josh Bersin, a longtime observer of human resources trends, has described Microsoft's program as something closer to a new management model than a traditional layoff.

"What Microsoft has done is not a layoff, rather a thoughtful workforce innovation, one which many companies will want to copy."

The AI connection

Both Microsoft and Alphabet, like almost all major technology companies, are spending enormous amounts to expand their AI ambitions.

To put money into AI, these companies are having to cut costs somewhere. Reducing employee headcount is one of the ways these giant corporations are doing so.

Bersin argues that this is not necessarily a sign of financial weakness.

"This is not the behavior of a company in distress: it's the behavior of a company thinking ahead."

"By creating space for self-selection out of the organization, they [Microsoft] make room to redeploy talent into AI-critical roles, continuing to hire selectively in high-growth areas, and maintain the engagement of those who stay."

In an era of heavy AI investment, corporate leaders face growing pressure to improve productivity metrics, including revenue per employee.

A measured reduction in headcount, achieved through voluntary means, can support those numbers while companies continue to fund their infrastructure buildout.

Bersin sees the approach as a logical response to the dual demands of technological ambition and financial discipline.

What comes next?

The deeper question is: Where are we headed?

Is this a temporary adjustment, a way for companies to finance enormous AI investments without destroying profitability?

Or is it the early version of a more permanent model, in which large technology firms continuously reshape their workforces through voluntary programs rather than following the old cycle of aggressive hiring followed by abrupt job cuts?

Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the International Monetary Fund, has warned that AI is "like a tsunami hitting the labor market."

IMF research has found that AI is likely to affect around 60% of jobs in advanced economies and 40% globally.

Dario Amodei, CEO of the IPO-bound Anthropic, has predicted that AI could eliminate half of all white-collar jobs and push unemployment to 20%.

A recent study from Stanford Digital Economy Lab, however, found that AI is not yet causing widespread, economy-wide job displacement, but is aggressively squeezing young workers.

There is a firm belief among many that human judgment will continue to be key.

"The idea that companies will no longer need people is an oversimplification. Human judgment, creativity, customer understanding and accountability remain essential," Bajrang Saharan, CEO of Pressmate OS, told Indian publication India Today.

Even amid gloomy forecasts, the World Economic Forum projects that 170 million new roles will emerge over the same period, resulting in a net gain of 78 million jobs worldwide.

However, WEF also cautions that entry-level jobs remain under immense pressure. It believes that "globally, more than one in three young workers are employed in occupations with medium to high exposure to AI-driven task change."

But one thing is for sure. Change is the only constant, and in the age of AI, that change is happening as rapidly as ever.

What has already changed is the signal these programs send. For much of the past half-century, a large voluntary buyout usually meant a company was in trouble.

How far that redefinition reaches will help determine the texture of work in the technology industry for years to come.

data.title: Airbnb stock analysis after boosting its revenue and profit guidance
data.description:
Airbnb stock jumped to its highest point since November 2021 after the company published strong financial results. It jumped to $193, up by 136% from its lowest point on record, with its valuation rising to over $110 billion. This rally may continue in the near future. 

Airbnb published strong financial results

ABNB stock continued its strong rally after releasing its third-quarter earnings report. This report showed that its revenue jumped by 19% to $4.9 billion, with its net income soaring by 38% to $1.9 billion. These numbers were better than what most analysts were expecting. 

Most notably, the company said that its free cash flow (FCF) rising by nearly 30% to $1.4 billion, with the gross booking value hitting $27.7 billion. These numbers showed that its revenue growth gained momentum, which is rare for a company of its size. 

The company also hinted that the growth will continue in the coming quarters, helped by its innovation. It now expects that its fourth-quarter revenue will jump to between $3.22 billion and $3.28 billion, up by between 16% and 18%. These metrics were better than the average estimate of $3.16 billion.

For the year, the company is expected to grow in the high teens, higher than what analysts were expecting. Analysts were expecting its annual revenue to come in at $14.18 billion. These are encouraging numbers for a company that has not made any acquisitions. 

Instead, the management has continued to innovate, including by allowing hotels to add their rooms to the platform. Thousands of boutique and independent hotels have already signed up so far. It has also added car rentals, which have become popular among users, and partnered with American Express. It also partnered with Meta Platform to use Muse agent.

Analysts have reacted positively to the earnings. Ygal Arounian, a Wedbush analyst, hiked his target from $200 to $237, suggesting a 40% upside. Shyam Patil of Susquehanna hiked the forecast from $200 to $220, while Rosenblatt increased it from $220 to $230. Other analysts who have upgraded the stock recently are from companies like Cantor Fitzgerald, Raymond James, and UBS Group.

Some of these analysts note that the strong growth will help to justify its relatively high valuation. Kyro datashows that the company has a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 32, which is higher than the sector median of 16.

Airbnb stock technical analysis

ABNB stock chart | Source: TradingView

The daily chart shows that the ABNB stock bottomed at $149.5 in September and then started an uptrend. It formed an up-gap today after publishing its financial results.

The stock has moved above the 50-day and 100-day Exponential Moving Averages (EMA). It has also moved above the Supertrend indicator and the median line of the Andrews pitchfork tool.

The stock will likely continue rising in the coming days as investors target the key resistance level of $200. This view will be confirmed if it jumps above the intraday high of $193.

The post Airbnb stock analysis after boosting its revenue and profit guidance appeared first on Invezz

data.title: Nasdaq rebounds 1% as chip stocks recover; Dow falls despite strong jobs data
data.description:
US stocks opened higher on Friday as chipmakers and technology stocks recovered from Thursday’s sharp selloff.

The Nasdaq Composite led the rebound, while Dow Jones remained under pressure, as investors assessed stronger-than-expected jobs data and concerns about potential restrictions on AI infrastructure development.

The recovery followed a bruising session on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq Composite entered correction territory after its steepest one-day decline in 19 months.

Investors were also weighing the implications of the October employment report and the outlook for interest rates.

Chip stocks lead recovery after Thursday's rout

The Nasdaq Composite opened 1% higher while the S&P 500 gained 0.35%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, however, fell 476 points.

Nvidia rose 5.64% in trading after losing 9% on Thursday, its worst session since January 2025.

Micron Technology gained 5.3% after falling 17% in the previous session.

AMD, Intel and Broadcom also advanced between 5% and 9%.

Data-centre operators IREN and Applied Digital, cloud computing companies CoreWeave and Nebius Group, and energy and equipment suppliers GE Vernova and Constellation Energy also recovered from steep losses.

Tesla and SpaceX shares rose 1.5% and 5%, respectively, after declining sharply over the previous two sessions.

Software company Atlassian moved in the opposite direction, falling 11.5% after reporting its first-quarter results.

Airbnb gained 10.39% after raising its full-year 2026 revenue growth forecast.

The rebound followed Thursday’s broad market decline.

The Nasdaq fell 5.5%, moving more than 10% below its recent high and entering correction territory. The S&P 500 lost 4.4%, while the Dow dropped more than 1,800 points, or 3.4%.

All 11 S&P 500 sectors ended lower.

The Magnificent Seven companies collectively lost $1 trillion in market capitalisation during the session.

AI regulation concerns weigh on market sentiment

The selloff was driven partly by concerns that Democratic gains in the midterm elections could lead to tighter restrictions on data-centre development.

Democratic victories in several key states and control of Congress raised questions about the pace of the AI infrastructure buildout.

Texas, a major data-centre hub, became a particular focus after Governor-Elect Gina Hinojosa indicated that the state would seek stronger protections before allowing further development.

The concerns weighed heavily on semiconductor companies and other businesses exposed to AI infrastructure.

The Nasdaq was also heading for its fourth consecutive weekly decline, while the S&P 500 was on track for its worst weekly performance since March 2025.

The CBOE Volatility Index, Wall Street’s fear gauge, recorded its largest one-day jump in about 19 months on Thursday. It eased slightly on Friday to 26.81.

Strong jobs report puts interest rate outlook in focus

Investors also assessed October employment data, which showed that US nonfarm payrolls increased by 165,000, well above economists’ expectations of 59,000.

The unemployment rate declined to 4.1%, compared with forecasts for it to remain at 4.2%.

The stronger labour market data pushed Treasury yields higher and limited gains in equity markets.

Investors are also monitoring the Federal Reserve’s next policy decision, with traders pricing in a more than 76% chance of an interest rate hike in December, according to the CME FedWatch Tool.

Oil prices added another source of uncertainty after rising on Thursday, raising concerns about energy-driven inflation and the possibility of higher interest rates.

Brent crude futures were broadly flat on Friday, although oil remained on course for a sharp weekly decline.

Despite Friday’s recovery, the Nasdaq and S&P 500 remained down around 4.4% and nearly 3%, respectively, for the week through Thursday.

The Dow was relatively more resilient, with a weekly decline of about 0.5%.

AI disclosure: AI tools assisted with research and drafting of this piece. An Invezz editor reviewed the facts, sources and wording before publication. Any opinions or analysis are Invezz’s, not those of an automated system.

The post Nasdaq rebounds 1% as chip stocks recover; Dow falls despite strong jobs data appeared first on Invezz
